name: Gareth Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. What's a normal shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, a junior operator loading flat glass into a tempering furnace. I finished secondary school and still ask the lead about the cooling setting. A clear pane coming through straight is satisfying; moving a bowed rack back for rework is the tiring part.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner schedules drivers at a courier depot, and we have two school-age children, seven and twelve, and a mortgage. The evening premium makes my factory pay higher than usual. We have about eight months of expenses saved and plenty of similar plants nearby. I use AI now and then to explain alarm codes, then check the furnace manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the glass crew AI can clean up a delivery note, but the furnace still needs somebody to notice a warped pane before it is packed. A neat label will not straighten bad glass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My evening premium makes this a well-paid junior job, and my partner's dispatch pay is steady. We have about eight months of expenses saved, a mortgage and two children. Plenty of other plants hire nearby, so a mild change feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep loading panes onto the tempering furnace conveyor and checking the first piece with the lead. I use AI now and then to explain an alarm code, but check the furnace manual before changing a setting. We'll add fresh money from full pay months to the children's savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I have a useful machine skill to build and no reason to expect our wages to shrink in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened with the bowed pane?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pane from last week's run bowed after the furnace cooled unevenly. The lead showed me the straightedge check, and we held that rack before it went to packing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you separate your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children are seven and twelve. We save for their school costs only after the mortgage and food are paid, because the existing eight-month reserve is for an interruption, not for every new purchase.

The **first tempered pane** should be inspected before packing.
think: Our two **steady wages** and eight-month reserve cover current bills.
Plenty of **nearby plants** offer options if the furnace job changes.
do: **Keep** loading and checking panes with the lead operator.
**Add** new wage money for the children after essential bills.
feel: **Calm** about paid factory work under mild software change.
S0.quote: A neat label will not straighten bad glass.
fieldNote: Gareth uses **AI occasionally** for alarm words, but relies on the manual and a straightedge.
The **strong cushion** and evening premium support calm, with new saving from earned wages.

steps.text: Keep loading tempering furnace and checking first glass panes
Add new full-wage money to children school account after bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the factory that AI may plan courier routes before robots handle hot glass. The company should try a revised furnace schedule against real cooling time before it shortens a paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner schedules drivers at a courier depot, so the planning and booking tasks on the card could cut those paid hours first. Eight months saved gives us time, but I don't want to live on it. My own furnace work remains hands-on for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner will ask the depot for a written dispatch-hours plan. If our plant offers a paid supervised lesson on the new AI cooling scheduler, I'll learn how to correct a run using measured pane temperatures, after another line has proved it. I'll compare four paid rosters before we replace our ageing car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible reduction in household pay, even while my own shift looks safe. I'd rather have the real dispatch roster than an assurance that software creates opportunities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the cooling scheduler?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enter the actual cooling minutes from three glass racks and check whether the screen allows a quality hold before packing. If the cooling screen cuts the quality hold, the old furnace schedule stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why delay replacing the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car still runs safely, so waiting costs us little. If dispatch hours fall, we will put that money toward mortgage and school transport instead of a replacement vehicle.

**Delay** car replacement while dispatch pay is uncertain.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic household wage loss.

fieldNote: The **new AI learning** is correction of a cooling schedule, beyond his occasional alarm-code questions.
The paid session remains **conditional on an offer** and proof from actual glass racks.

steps.text: Ask courier depot for written paid dispatch-hours plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2028 could plan courier routes, and capable robots around 2031 could lift and inspect hot glass. I'd tell my neighbours the worker needs safe retraining before anyone sells a factory machine as a complete wage plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when physical robots reach the furnace. My partner's dispatch hours might shrink sooner, and my own higher evening premium could go if the loading crew is smaller. Eight months saved and many nearby plants give options, but a mortgage needs a continuing wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week we'll seek written staffing plans from the courier depot and glass factory. If the factory offers a funded paid-time furnace-maintenance course with a real supervised place on a cooled, guarded line, I'll enrol. If qualified and my shifts are cut, I'll apply to posted local maintenance jobs only when safe duties, regular hours and base pay meet our costs; if no course is offered, I'll apply to posted local glass-operator jobs with adequate pay and school-compatible hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible cuts to both wages, but I can use the reserve and nearby job market while looking for a real offer. I do not expect to lose everything next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would safe maintenance training cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The trainer should isolate the conveyor, prove the furnace section has cooled and gauge a robot-moved test pane. I would want to practise stopping a rack before it tips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you compare another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the advertised base wage with our mortgage, school transport and food, then check the shift time against child collection. A maintenance title without base pay and school-compatible hours is no decision.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes courier routing before robots handle glass around 2031.
Workers need **paid guarded furnace training** and actual staffing plans.
think: At **48**, a smaller furnace crew could cost my evening premium.
Eight months of **savings** and many local plants provide options, not guaranteed equal pay.
do: **Seek** written courier and furnace staffing plans this week.
**Enrol** in paid guarded maintenance training if real funded place offered.
**Apply** for posted safe local work if qualified, shifts cut and pay suffices.
feel: **Anxious** about possible two-wage reductions with time to act.
S2.quote: A maintenance title without base pay and school-compatible hours is no decision.
fieldNote: He requests **written plans** and an offered paid safe course before treating maintenance as a path.
The **qualified maintenance application** and no-course glass fallback are separate, posted and pay-dependent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If thinking AI changes courier routing in 2031 and capable robots handle panes around 2034, I'd tell the plant five years is enough to test a guarded furnace route. Workers should see a real job at the end of any training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when robots can do the physical loading. Our children will be older, but the mortgage may still need both wages. A five-year lead lets me build maintenance experience while the evening premium is still paid, if a course place is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the furnace shift and add new money from full evening-premium months to savings. If the plant offers a recognized maintenance course with fees covered, paid release and hands-on practice on a cooled guarded line, I'll enrol next year. After qualifying, if either wage falls, I'll apply only to posted local maintenance roles with safe duties and enough regular hours and base pay for our costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household wage risk, but I can make a measured move with five years. I would not leave a good furnace rate for a training advert alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would practical assessment involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd practise checking a furnace thermocouple, stopping the conveyor and measuring a pane after a guarded robot lift. An instructor needs to watch the first attempt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a posting need to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A job posting must state the ordinary rate and hours, not only overtime. If the new role pays less than our bills, I will keep the present paid shift while looking elsewhere.

feel: **Anxious** about future household wages with a longer preparation path.
S3.quote: I would not leave a good furnace rate for a training advert alone.
fieldNote: New **saving** comes from future paid premium months, not the existing eight-month reserve.
The **application** requires qualification, an actual wage cut, safe local duties and adequate posted base pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2036 could handle courier routes, and capable robots around 2039 could move and inspect hot glass. I'd tell my children a decade gives us time to build skills, but a glossy demo still needs a real pane test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when hands-on robots reach the furnace. My children may be grown, but the mortgage and living costs could still need my wage. The eight-month reserve and nearby plants help us make decisions; they do not guarantee a shift in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the furnace wage and put fresh money from each full premium month into savings. Each year we'll compare our mortgage balance with actual local job postings. If the plant offers a funded paid-time maintenance certificate with cooled guarded practice, I'll take it; if robotics later cuts my hours, I'll apply after qualifying only to safe posted local jobs with regular pay and hours that cover our costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a later wage change, while our household pay looks secure today. A decade lets me wait for a proved machine before committing to a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe robot lift test include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would test a robot lift on a cooled rack, with the stop control in reach and a gauge check on the first pane. A perfect digital count cannot show a bowed glass edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a future advert need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the job advert to name the pay, shift and certificate required. If no paid course place or suitable posting appears, I'll keep earning on the current line as long as it operates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 picture worries me most. Courier dispatch hours could shrink before robots reach my glass furnace around 2031, and the evening premium matters to our mortgage. Written crew plans, offered paid guarded maintenance training and a posted local job with adequate base pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who measures the first pane after a robot moves it from the furnace. A glass edge can be bowed even when the machine's count is perfect.

headlineQuote: A glass edge can be bowed even when the machine's count is perfect.
portrait: **Gareth**, 43, is a junior glass-furnace operator with secondary school education and a high evening rate.
He and his courier-dispatch partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with eight months of expenses saved.
He uses **AI occasionally** for alarms and waits for a proved paid lesson before learning new controls.
The partner’s exposed **dispatch hours** make slower disruption anxious despite strong savings and plentiful nearby plants.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut dispatch pay before capable robots reach his glass line around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing plans**, offered paid guarded maintenance training and posted safe local work at enough base pay would help.
